title: Sample size selection in optimization methods for machine learning
contribution: A batch-type method that grows the gradient sample when a sample-variance test of the descent condition fails, with linear convergence in expectation and O(1/epsilon) total work for an idealized geometric-growth variant, a Newton-CG method whose CG stop test balances the residual against the estimated Hessian subsampling error, and a two-phase subsampled-Hessian Newton-CG method for L1 problems, tested on Google speech data (preprint pp. 4-6, 12-17, 22-25).
problem_entry: Parallel computing changes the SGD-versus-batch trade-off; Bottou-Bousquet's 'SGD is to be preferred' analysis does not cover dynamic batches; [7] fixed the gradient sample and CG count; L1 models need second-order sparse methods (pp. 2-3, 6-7, 15, 21-22).
key_idea: Replace the unavailable test ||grad J_S - grad J|| <= theta ||grad J_S|| by its variance form and size the next sample from it (3.9)-(3.12); stop CG when the residual reaches the variance-estimated Hessian sampling error (5.6); L1: OWL's orthant rule read as a gradient-projection step, Newton-CG on free variables, OWL's alignment step dropped (pp. 4-5, 15-17, 22-25).
assumptions: Linear prediction w^T x, convex loss (p. 3); J twice differentiable and uniformly convex (4.2), admitted as a limitation for logistic loss (pp. 7, 10); fixed step because Armijo is 'more difficult to analyze' (p. 7); bounded per-sample variance omega (4.22) and imposed growth n_k = a^k (p. 11); N -> infinity / sampling with replacement (p. 5); fixed sample in the L1 part (p. 22).
proof_devices: relative gradient-accuracy condition implies descent: grad J^T g >= (1-theta)||g||^2 (4.14), then Taylor with step (1-theta)/L gives J_{k+1} <= J_k - (beta/L)||grad J_k||^2 (4.16) (pp. 8-9)
gradient-dominance inequality ||grad J||^2 >= lambda (J - J*) from uniform convexity via the averaged Hessian H_k (4.3)-(4.5) (pp. 7-8)
deriving the analysable sample-growth rate: imposing the variance test with bound (4.12) forces n_k >= O((1-beta lambda/L)^-k), so geometric growth (4.23) is imposed (p. 11)
induction on E[J(w_k)-J*] <= C rho^k with rho = max{1-lambda/(4L), 1/a}, using E||g||^2 = ||grad J||^2 + ||Var(g)||_1 and Var(g) <= omega/n_k (Theorem 4.2, p. 12)
total work by summing a geometric series of sample sizes; choosing a <= (1-lambda/(4L))^-1 makes tau = 1; any overestimate of kappa suffices (Corollary 4.3, pp. 13-14)
bound comparison with Bottou-Bousquet under the approximation nu-bar ~ omega/lambda: kappa versus kappa^2 (Table 4.1, p. 14)
experiments: One Google speech problem (N = 168,776, m = 10,191): dynamic Algorithm 5.2 against its static predecessor at |S| = N and 0.05N, R = 0.1, S0 = 1%, theta = 0.5, x-axis accessed data points (pp. 18-19); estimator-versus-truth Table 5.1 over 17 iterations (p. 20); four theta values (pp. 20-21); L1 problem (N = 191,607, m = 30,315) against OWL from LibLBFGS at memory 5 and 20 (pp. 24-25); single runs, no SGD baseline; figure curves not in the text layer.
positioning: Extends [7] (Byrd, Chin, Neveitt, Nocedal 2011) (pp. 2-3, 15); answers Bottou-Bousquet's preference for SGD with a competitive bound (pp. 6-7, 14); says OWL's convergence proof 'is not correct' (Proposition 4) and recasts OWL as gradient projection (pp. 24-27); dismisses Shapiro-Homem-de-Mello's confidence-ellipsoid rule as infeasible at scale; related work placed last (p. 27).
writing: Three-part abstract (p. 1); practical algorithm and analysed variant separated explicitly (pp. 6, 15); measured hedges in the body ('reasonably accurate', 'only moderately faster', pp. 20, 25) but a stronger 'outperform' in the final remarks (p. 28); one-sentence justification for each design choice (pp. 15, 22); slip 'Theorem 6.1' for Theorem 4.1 (p. 11).
limits_future: Stated: dynamic sampling for L1 deferred to 'a future paper' (pp. 22, 28); a better gradient-projection active-set search deferred as 'not simple' (p. 27); uniform convexity (p. 10). Unstated: theory covers only the idealized variant; no convergence result for the L1 method after the alignment safeguard is dropped; one data set, single runs, no SGD comparison (pp. 15, 18-27).

method_links.note: Classical gradient / Newton-CG engine with line search kept; only the sample-size decision and the CG stopping test are made regime-aware, each driven by an explicit sample-variance estimate. Recovery is missing: the sample only grows.
Bottou-Bousquet's 'SGD is to be preferred' put on trial with a competitive bound for a dynamic batch method; OWL's convergence-motivated alignment step dropped because it slows the iteration.

Theory is for an idealized variant (fixed step 1/L, imposed a^k growth), not the variance-test algorithm that is run; a complexity bound is used to argue competitiveness with SGD; no convergence result for the L1 method.
Cost counted in accessed data points and the rival OWL run from a public third-party code at two memory sizes, but one problem, one run, no self-handicap, and the SGD rival absent from experiments.

Deferred items (dynamic sampling for L1, better active-set prediction) written down as future papers; later l1 second-order works S087 (2015) and S089 (2016) exist in INDEX.md; link inferred from titles only, those papers not read here.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: CG is stopped when its residual reaches the estimated Hessian subsampling error along the first CG direction, scaled by ||d_j||^2/||p_0||^2, since extra accuracy 'may not lead to an improved search direction'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Re-derive a rival heuristic as a classical method
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: OWL's orthant selection recast as a gradient-projection step, which 'has the advantage of suggesting variants of the algorithm and mechanisms for establishing global convergence'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Computable proxy for an unavailable quantity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sample variance with finite-population correction stands in for the unavailable gradient error, and is validated against the truth in Table 5.1.

transferable: Replace an unavailable relative-accuracy test ||g - grad J|| <= theta ||g|| by its variance form ||Var_S||_1/|S| <= theta^2 ||g||^2 and size the next sample from the same inequality (pp. 4-5).
Stop CG when ||r_j||^2 <= gamma ||d_j||^2, with gamma the per-sample variance of Hessian-vector products along p_0 over |H| ||p_0||^2, computed once per outer iteration (pp. 16-17).
Fix the Hessian/gradient sample ratio so that CG Hessian-vector cost stays below one gradient evaluation, removing a tuning parameter (p. 15).

To analyse a test-driven sampler, derive the growth rate the test forces under bounded variance and analyse the idealized variant imposing that rate; total work follows from a geometric sum (pp. 11-14).
Tabulate an estimator against the true quantity over a real run before relying on it (Table 5.1, p. 20).
Plot all methods against accessed data points (function, gradient and Hessian-vector products together) (p. 19).
coauthors: Richard H. Byrd, Gillian M. Chin, Yuchen Wu

quotes.text: The focus of this section is on the development of a practical algorithm, not on establishing complexity bounds, and therefore our method is an extension of Algorithm 3.1 and not of the idealized variant given by (4.23)-(4.24).
The alignment is motivated by the need to achieve global convergence properties, but our computational experience indicates that it slows down the iteration.

title: An interior point method for nonlinear programming with infeasibility detection capabilities
contribution: Two-phase (optimality / feasibility) interior-point methods for NLP, built into KNITRO as extensions of knitro/cg and knitro/direct, that use the normal component of a step-decomposition step to decide when to switch to an l1 feasibility barrier problem, with hysteresis rules against cycling; infeasibility detection rises from 8/17 to 17/17 (CG) and 11/17 to 14/17 (line search) on small infeasible problems, with essentially unchanged termination on 430 CUTEr problems (manuscript pp. 5-17; counts mine).
problem_entry: Infeasible NLPs arise in parameter sweeps and in branch-and-bound subproblems run thousands of times; a NEOS snapshot of ten solver/algorithm combinations shows the authors' own interior codes knitro/direct and knitro/cg 'quite poor' at detecting infeasibility (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: The normal step of the Byrd-Omojokun-type step decomposition estimates the attainable first-order infeasibility reduction theta(x), which line-search primal-dual methods cannot measure; switch to a feasibility mode when the linearized residual is >= 0.9 ||c|| and back when <= 0.1 ||c||, keeping the knitro/cg engine, merit function and penalty update unchanged (pp. 2, 5-8).
assumptions: Smooth f, g, h (p. 4); infeasibility measure w = (g+, h) (p. 4); the run starts assuming a feasible solution exists (p. 9); no convergence assumptions because no analysis is given (p. 16); constants delta, delta-bar and IPM initialization admitted as sensitive (pp. 10, 12).
proof_devices: first-order characterization of an infeasible stationary point, ||w(x)|| > 0 and theta(x) = 0 for any trust radius (3.3), turned into the relative test theta(x_k) <= delta ||w(x_k)|| (p. 5)
termination by KKT residuals of the NLP and of the feasibility problem; ||w|| > 0 at a stationary point of (4.10) accepted as a certificate of local infeasibility (p. 9)
LICQ-failure exit relying on Theorem 3 of Byrd-Gilbert-Nocedal [3] (p. 9)
no theorems proved; convergence analysis deferred to a future study (p. 16)
experiments: Section 2: SNOPT, FILTER, KNITRO 7.0 (active/CG/direct), IPOPT, LANCELOT, MINOS on NEOS/AMPL defaults over 17 infeasible problems (LOQO, PENNON detected none); iteration units differ by solver (pp. 3-4). Section 5: KNITRO 8.0, alg=2, presolve=0, maxiter=3000, maxtime_real=500, bar_switchrule 1 vs 2; Table 4 detection 8/17 -> 17/17 (p. 13); Table 5 terminations on 430 CUTEr problems, Morales log2 iteration ratios on 391 (pp. 13-14). Section 6 line search: Table 6 11/17 -> 14/17 with a powellbs regression not discussed; Table 7 terminations (p. 17). No CPU time; full per-problem tables in Appendices A-B (pp. 20-35).
positioning: Surveys infeasibility handling across SNOPT, FILTER, Gould-Robinson, Byrd-Curtis-Nocedal steering, Yamashita-Yabe, Chin-Fletcher, LOQO, IPOPT, Curtis, LANCELOT and MINOS; asserts it is 'distinct' without detailed argument; credits FILTER's restoration phase and judges IPOPT's 'not consistently successful'; one citation slip ('Curtis [2]' points to the Byrd-Curtis-Nocedal TR) (pp. 2, 4, 17).
writing: Short pseudo-code-centred body; one-line verdicts ('It is clear that...', 'no loss of robustness') (p. 13); 'solid theoretical underpinning' claimed without proof (p. 12); plain self-criticism of the authors' own codes (p. 4); two-sentence final remarks (p. 16); constants introduced as delta-bar > delta but set 0.9 and 0.1 in the reverse order (p. 8).
limits_future: Stated: convergence analysis left for a future study (p. 16); sensitivity to delta, delta-bar handled by extra rules (p. 12); IPM initialization sensitivity (p. 10). Future: a feasible interior method in feasibility mode that keeps satisfied inequalities satisfied and drops the relaxation variables (p. 17). Unstated: small infeasible test sets (n <= 251), iterations only, line-search losses left in tables (pp. 3, 17).

method_links.note: KNITRO's known failure mode (no infeasibility handling in its interior algorithms, Tables 2-3) becomes the paper and ships as KNITRO extensions selected by the option bar_switchrule=2; the paper's own diagnosis restates the 2006 KNITRO limitation, supporting the timing-inferred arrow in SKILL.md.

Step-decomposition engine kept; mode control added, driven by an explicit estimate of the best attainable feasibility progress (normal-step linearized reduction versus ||c||), with a return-to-main recovery test and exits for infeasible stationary points and LICQ failure.

The snapshot prints the authors' own codes losing and credits FILTER; old and new compared inside one code base with identical options except the switch rule. Caveats: iteration units differ across solvers, line-search losses only in tables, no CPU time.
The line-search capability is built on knitro/direct's existing fallback to the knitro/cg step-decomposition algorithm; the integrated architecture makes the extension cheap.
Practice first: theory is a one-line stationarity characterization, convergence analysis promised for a future study.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Minimal-progress test (zeta = 0.99), at least 3 main-mode iterations, two consecutive triggers, and a (1 - sigma) infeasibility decrease before returning, so that delta and delta-bar need no adjustment during the run.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Self-exposing snapshot benchmark on a purpose-built failure set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A group-built collection of infeasible problems (Test Set 2, Curtis-Oztoprak TR [12]) run on all major codes, the authors' own included, before the method is proposed; own interior codes shown 'quite poor'.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Computable proxy for an unavailable quantity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The normal step's predicted linearized feasibility reduction stands in for the first-order stationarity measure theta(x) of the feasibility problem.

transferable: Turn a stationarity characterization of the bad outcome into a relative switching test that the step computation evaluates for free (pp. 5, 8).
Choose the algorithm architecture whose by-products measure what the new feature needs (step decomposition rather than line-search primal-dual, because only it yields theta(x)) (pp. 2, 5).

Give every mode switch explicit warm-start rules: barrier parameter carried over, trust radius rescaled by sqrt(n+m+2t)/sqrt(n), penalty and multipliers inherited or recomputed by least squares (pp. 10, 12).
Protect a heuristic switch with dwell-time and two-consecutive-trigger rules (p. 12).

Show a robustness feature is harmless with a full old-by-new termination cross-table over the standard set, then compare iterations only where both runs reach the same objective (Tables 5, 7, pp. 13-14, 17).
For two-code comparisons use the per-problem log2 iteration ratio rather than performance profiles (p. 13).

quotes.text: The performance of the interior point methods knitro/direct and knitro/cg are quite poor, which may not be surprising since these two algorithms do not contain any features for handling infeasibility.
We have found that these additional switching rules prevent the algorithm from switching modes too rapidly, and also make it unnecessary to try to adjust the values of the constants

title: On large-batch training for deep learning: Generalization gap and sharp minima
contribution: An empirical study across six networks showing that large-batch ADAM reaches training accuracy similar to small-batch ADAM but lower testing accuracy, and that its solutions are 1-2 orders of magnitude sharper by a box-constrained sensitivity metric computed with a few L-BFGS-B iterations; warm-start, batch-size and distance probes attribute the gap to lack of exploration and gradient noise, and four remedies only partly help (arXiv v2 pp. 3-9, 13-16).
problem_entry: Practitioners observe a generalization drop with larger batches, which blocks the parallelism that large batches would allow; the gap is measured at up to 5% and its cause is asked for (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Large-batch methods converge to sharp minimizers and small-batch methods to flat ones because gradient noise ejects iterates from sharp basins; tested with 1-D parametric plots, a sharpness metric, a batch-size sweep, warm-started large-batch runs and distance-from-x0 ratios against four enumerated conjectures (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Finite-sum nonconvex training (p. 1); SB = ADAM with 256 points, LB = ADAM with 10% of the data, trained until the loss stops improving (p. 4); 'minimizer' used loosely for the final iterate (p. 5); the sharpness-generalization link taken from flat-minima, MDL and Bayesian literature, not tested (p. 3); metric 'although imperfect', spectral reading for small epsilon (pp. 5-6).
proof_devices: box-constrained sharpness metric with half-widths epsilon(|(A+x)_i| + 1) for invariance to dimension and sparsity, in full space and random 100-dimensional subspaces (pp. 5-6)
spectral interpretation: metric relates to the largest Hessian eigenvalue (A = I) or a projected Ritz value (random A) (p. 6)
idealized parallel performance model I_l/I_s < B_s/(f_s(P) B_l) (App. C, p. 13)
experiments: Six networks (MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100; fully connected, AlexNet-like, VGG-like), 5 random starts with mean +/- std (p. 4); accuracy Table 2 (p. 4); sharpness Tables 3-4 with two epsilon values (pp. 6-7); parametric plots from one SB/LB pair (pp. 5-6, 14); batch-size sweep (pp. 7-8); warm-start from 100 SB epochs (p. 7-8); remedies: data augmentation (Table 6), conservative training (Table 7), adversarial and stability training (no benefit) (pp. 13-16). Claims for other optimizers and networks given without data (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Builds on Hochreiter-Schmidhuber flat minima, MDL, MacKay and Chaudhari et al. (p. 3) and Goodfellow et al.'s visualization; sets aside Ferris's convex-analysis 'sharp minimum' (p. 5); reports alignment with loss-surface theory (p. 9); borrows remedies from ML practice and offers the group's own dynamic sampling (Byrd et al. 2012 = S018) as a prospective remedy (pp. 9, 15-16).
writing: Boxed main observation (p. 3); asymmetric hedging between the abstract ('as is well known', p. 1) and the body ('loosely', 'apparently', 'only provided some numerical evidence', pp. 5, 7, 9); lettered open questions (p. 9); figures carry the argument; slips: conservative-training results said to be in 'Figure 7' (Table 7) and C2 described as 'The C3 network' (pp. 12, 15).
limits_future: Stated: numerical evidence only (p. 9); remedies 'do not completely remedy the problem' (pp. 6, 9); performance model idealized (p. 13); open questions (a)-(e) on proof, density of minima, architectures, initialization and steering LB away from sharp minimizers (p. 9); dynamic sampling as a future remedy (p. 9). Unstated: second-order optimality never checked; parametric plots from one pair; augmented LB matching or beating SB on C2 and C4 played down (pp. 5, 13-14).

method_links.note: In the body the work keeps what it cannot prove as lettered open questions and says it offers numerical evidence, not proof (step 5).

Four rival explanations are put on trial and over-fitting is ruled out with data, but the sharpness-generalization link is adopted as 'well known' and the study ends supporting 'a commonly held view'; context of SKILL.md warning sign 8.

Like-with-like comparison (one optimizer, 5 runs, mean +/- std), but claims about other optimizers and networks have no data and augmented-LB results that match or beat SB are played down in the text.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Numbered rival conjectures (i)-(iv), each experiment tied to the conjecture it supports or rules out (training/testing curves against over-fitting, warm-start probe, distance ratios).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Computable proxy for an unavailable quantity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sharpness computed by a few L-BFGS-B iterations on a box-constrained maximization instead of Hessian eigenvalues, with a spectral interpretation; here a diagnostic only, unlike the algorithm-driving proxies of S018 and S053.

transferable: Measure sensitivity as the relative rise of f maximized over a box epsilon(|x_i| + 1) around the solution, in the full space and in random subspaces, solved inexactly by a fixed small number of L-BFGS-B iterations, at two epsilon values (pp. 5-7).
Rule out over-fitting before claiming another mechanism by showing testing accuracy has no peak-then-decay over epochs (pp. 4-5).
Probe a basin hypothesis with warm starts: run the competing regime from the other regime's iterate at each epoch and plot accuracy and the diagnostic against the warm-start epoch (pp. 7-8).
Sweep the controlling parameter and plot outcome and diagnostic on twin axes to locate a threshold (pp. 7-8).
Report the distance travelled from x0 by each regime as a cheap test of the nearest-minimizer conjecture (p. 9).
Report failed remedies with the same metrics as successful ones (pp. 15-16).
